string.text: Siegeberht patrols the borders of Rohan.
Éowyn, Lady of Rohan, is sister to Éomer and niece to Théoden. She slew the Witch-King at the Pelennor, striking down the terror of the ages.
Théodwyn was sister to King Théoden and mother of Éomer and Éowyn. She died of grief after her husband Éomund was slain by Orcs.
Elfgrim serves as a rider of the royal household.
Éomund of the Eastfold rode as Marshal of the Mark and wed Théodwyn, sister of the king. Orcs cut him down in the Emyn Muil, and his two children passed into Théoden's keeping.
Ailinel, spouse to Oropherion, embodies the graceful Sindar nobility, her strategic insights aiding in the clan's ancient rituals and alliances within the Woodland Realm.
Alenon, leader of Nos Alenwé, venerates the stars as the first elves did at Cuiviénen, using celestial lore to navigate and predict dangers in the star-obscured forest.
Amarië, spouse to Galenor, represents the enduring love themes in elven tales, her songs revitalizing the clan's spirits amid the growing gloom.
Anairë, a wise counselor in the clan, reflects the steadfast elven women in Tolkien's tales, guiding the kindred with visions of starlit paths.

Calion of the House of Eärnurionath keeps the sea-wall of Pelargir as his fathers did before him, since the days when the Faithful first laid stone upon that haven in the Second Age. He bears a long blade named Sîrlam, the River-Tongue, which his great-grandsire wielded at the breaking of the corsair fleet off Tolfalas. In these darkening years he has lent his voice and his ships to the cause of the King returned, holding that the oath of the Stewards was sworn until such a one should come, and come he has.

Silwen, brought in dower from a sister-house of Pelargir to the House of Eärnurionath, has the bearing of the sea-roads in her speech and the wariness of the haven-watch in her eye. She wedded Calion in the autumn of her three and thirtieth year, and to her dowry she added a chart of the southern shoals drawn by her grandsire who fell at the burning of the quays. With her husband she holds for the King returned, for she has seen, year upon year, how the Corsairs grow bold while the City waits, and waiting alone shall not now suffice.

Eleniel of the House of Barahirionath is but fourteen summers old, yet already she is named among the fairest maidens of Lossarnach, the Vale of Flowers. She is taught the old songs of plenty and the older songs of mourning, and her father's foresters have begun to school her in the axe-craft for which her vale is famed. Her house keeps faith with Lord Denethor, as the husbandmen of Lossarnach have ever kept faith with the City whose granaries they fill; the young lady knows no other loyalty, and asks none.

Nauriel of the House of Halboronionath, sixty winters told and the institutional memory of her line, dwells in the upland halls of Lamedon above the cold rush of Ciril. In her middle years she rode with the hillmen against the brigands of the high passes, and she yet keeps the dented helm of that summer upon the mantel of her hall. She is among the firmest voices for the King returned, holding with Angbor and the stubborn lords of the dales that the long waiting has worn the realm thin, and that the oath must at the last be honoured.

Calaniel was wedded into the House of Malandilionath out of the green wolds of Pinnath Gelin, and she brought with her the fair hair of Hirluin's country and a small banner of pale green that her mother stitched for her bridal-journey. She is eight and twenty, gentle of voice but not of purpose, and she has borne a son who shall one day raise the house's standard upon the western hills. With her husband's kindred she stands by the Steward of the City, for the green hills lie far from any northern claimant and near indeed to the beacons of Anórien.

Ciriondir of the House of Malandilionath, fourteen years of age, is the chosen heir of his father's hall in the green country of Pinnath Gelin. He is taught the bow and the long shepherd's stride, for the youths of his vale must outpace the wolf and the worse than wolf when the watch-fires are lit. Reared upon his father's knee in the loyalties of his house, he is sworn in his heart to Lord Denethor, and he counts the days until he may bear his green pennon eastward to the muster of the City.

Rondiel, wedded to Lord Rondamir, was born of a lesser branch of the House of Ecthelionath in Lossarnach, and brought to her husband's hall the gentle learning of the Vale of Flowers. She is versed in the Sindarin tongue and in the lore of healing herbs gathered ere the frost. Her marriage knit the stern hill-folk of Lamedon to the orchard-lords of the south, and she is held in honor as a Lady of measured counsel. With her lord, she stands faithful to Denethor son of Ecthelion.

Silmador, kinsman of Lord Rondamir and second of the hall, is reckoned the swiftest rider of the house and warden of its eastern marches toward the Mering Stream. He bears a coat of mail wrought in the smithies of Erech, bequeathed to him by his uncle who fell on the Pelennor of an older war. By his wedding to Galinwen of Pelargir he has drawn the salt-wind of the haven into the high vales. He holds, as his kinsman holds, with Denethor of the House of Húrin.

Galinwen came out of Pelargir, daughter of a shipwright-house of old Faithful blood that has watched the sea-roads against the Corsairs of Umbar since the days of Castamir's flight. By her hand the House of Hýarthulionath has gained tidings of every keel betwixt Ethir Anduin and the Bay of Belfalas. She wedded Silmador in the autumn of a year of fair harvest, binding hill to haven. In the present strife she follows her husband's house and the Steward's banner.

Galdirion, son of Rondamir and Rondiel, is but fourteen summers old, yet already the household masters at arms set him to the practice-blade each dawn upon the courtyard stones. He is grey-eyed as his father, and quiet in the manner of the old Númenórean stock, given to long readings of the Annals of the Stewards. The hall names him heir of Erech-march, though he has not yet ridden to war. Ere the Shadow is broken, men say, his hour shall be required of him.

Rondamir, head of the House of Hýarthulionath, holds the upland fastness of Erech-march in Lamedon, where his forefathers swore fealty to Mardil Voronwë in the dimming after Eärnur rode forth. Tall and grey-eyed in the old Númenórean mould, he bears the sword Calanril, drawn in his great-grandsire's hand at the Crossings of Erui. In this hour of sundering he holds firm to the Steward of Gondor, deeming the oath unbroken while the Tower of Ecthelion yet stands. Now, as the shadow grows long upon the Ephel Dúath, he summons his hillmen to the muster of Minas Tirith.

Nimriel, Lady of the House of Caladionath, was born in Anfalas of the windward stock of Langstrand, daughter of a huntsman-lord whose hawks were prized in the courts of Dol Amroth. She came to Eldorion's hall in her twentieth year, bringing the sea-wisdom of the coast and a keen falconer's eye that has more than once warned the watch ere the beacons were lit. She is of the elder Númenórean cast, fair-skinned and tall, and walks the battlements at evening as her lord walks the muster-yards. With Eldorion she stands faithful to Denethor son of Ecthelion.

Orlathiel, daughter of Eldorion and Nimriel, is two-and-twenty, and counted among the fairest of the ladies of the upper hall, grey-eyed and dark-haired in the manner of her father's line. She was schooled in the histories of the House of Húrin and in the songs of the Stewards, and rides with her husband's archers upon the long patrols toward the eastern fences. The folk of the hall name her the Lady of the Morning Watch. In the present sundering she follows her father's faith, and the Steward's banner.

Orlendir came from the Morthond Vale, of an archer-house that has kept the Stone of Erech in its long sight since the breaking of the oath of old. He is two-and-twenty years of age, dark of hair and quiet of bearing, reckoned the keenest bowman to ride beneath the banner of Caladionath. His marriage to Orlathiel bound the watchful Blackroot to the northern bulwark of Eldorion's hall. He holds, as his good-father holds, with the Steward of Gondor.

Laswen of the House of Olindurionath, three and fifty winters of age and the eldest sister of the present lord, is the keeper of the house's chronicles upon the rim of the Langstrand. From her seat above the grey strand she has counted the sails of three generations of corsairs, and she has written down the names of the watchmen who did not return. She is the steady voice of the King's cause within her hall, for she has weighed the long ledger of the coast's neglect and finds the Steward's keeping wanting.

Lothwen, dowager-aunt of the House of Imrazôrionath, has counted seventy and two winters upon the white cliffs of Belfalas, and her counsel is sought ere any voyage is undertaken or any betrothal sealed. In her youth she sailed with her brother to the haven of Edhellond and there, it is whispered, looked upon the last of the Elven mariners; the silver brooch she yet wears is the token of that meeting. She abides by the Steward of the City and chides any kinsman who would speak of a king unproven, for vigilance is the long virtue of her line.

Lothériel of the House of Imrazôrionath was born to the silver shores of Belfalas, where the sea-wind tempers the daughters of old Númenor as surely as the sword tempers the son. Though yet young in her years, she has thrice ridden with the Swan-Knights upon the watch of the southern roads, and the elder ladies of Dol Amroth name her quick of wit and steady of hand. Her house holds firm to Lord Denethor, for the City must not falter while the shadow grows long, and the oath of the Stewards is an oath of stone.

Silmariel, born of the lesser house of Tarondor in Lebennin, came to Garvirionath in her twenty-second summer bringing a dowry of fair river-meadows and the loyalty of pikemen of the Five Streams. She is a lady of soft speech and unbending mind, and the hearth-hall of Amon Din has prospered under her hand. In the matter of the Steward and the claimant from the North, she counsels her lord to keep faith with Minas Tirith ere all is sundered.

Nimethil, only daughter of Vorondir and Silmariel, was raised within sight of the beacon-fires and learned to ride ere she learned to weave. She is dark-haired and grey-eyed after the manner of her kindred, slender as a rowan and twice as proud. In the gathering quarrel she stands with her father for Denethor, though she has been heard to speak softly of the old prophecies of the king's return.

Rúmen of the line of Cirdacar rode out of Pinnath Gelin to wed Nimethil, bringing the green banner and the troth of shepherd-spears unto Garvirionath. Though yet young in years, he proved his valor at a skirmish nigh Cair Andros, where he held a broken ford against orc-scouts until the beacon-riders came. He follows his lord-father Vorondir in the cause of the Steward, and dreams of a sword-name of his own ere his beard is grown.

Vorondir, Lord of Garvirionath, holds the green vales of Anorien beneath the beacon of Amon Din, where his fathers have kept watch since the days of Steward Belecthor. Gallant in the saddle and grave in council, he bears Lossen, the silver sword forged at Pelargir for his grandsire who fell at the Crossings of Erui. In these dimming years he has set his oath unbroken with Lord Denethor, holding the old custodial bond above the rumour of a king out of the wild North. By day he rides the marches with Rohirric scouts; by night he watches the eastern stars and counts how long the shadow has grown.

Ciriel was born to the seafaring house of Lhanthir in Belfalas, and the salt of Dol Amroth is yet upon her speech though sixty-seven winters have passed since she rode inland to wed Amandir. She brought to Hirilionath the alliance of Swan-Knight kinsmen and a chest of pearls from the silver shore. In her age she counsels her lord and her son alike, and stands with Amandir for the King.

Pelamir, only son of Amandir and Ciriel, has stood three and forty years in the long shadow of his father, learning patience as other men learn the sword. He is grey already at the temples though his sire yet lives, and the hill-folk of Lamedon call him quietly the Waiting Lord. With Amandir he has declared for the king out of the North, and many say that when the old lord at last passes, Pelamir shall ride east at the claimant's banner without a backward glance.

Dorwen of the house of Maeglion in Morthond Vale came to Hirilionath bearing the troth of Blackroot bowmen and the stern watchfulness of her shadowed valley. She is grave of countenance and slow of word, and has borne her husband Pelamir one son and many years of patient stewardship while the old lord lingered. She follows the house in its turning toward the claimant, though she remembers the old oaths to the White Tower with sorrow.

Sarnion, son of Pelamir and Dorwen, is two and twenty and the youngest sword of Hirilionath, dark-haired and lean as a hill-hound. He was sent in his fifteenth year to foster with kinsmen in Morthond, that he might learn the bow of his mother's people alongside the spear of his father's. He follows his grandsire and his father in the cause of the King, and burns with the hot certainty of the young.

Amandir, Lord of Hirilionath, is the eldest of the Tier lords of Gondor, and his memory reaches back unto the boyhood of the Steward himself. His seat is at Ethring above the fords of the Ringlo, in upland Lamedon, where the hill-spearmen have served his house for nine generations. He bears the silver-on-sable banner of his fathers, and the long sword Tirnaith, named for a kinsman lost at the Dagorlad of old. In the matter of the king out of the North, Amandir has cast his weight with the claimant, holding that the Steward's oath was sworn until the king should come again, and that this hour, ere he himself passes, is that hour.

Balatar, cousin-german to Lord Amandir, has kept the lower hall of Ethring these forty years and is reckoned among the last men living who remembers the funeral of Steward Turgon. He is broad-shouldered yet, though his beard is wholly white, and the household captains seek him out for tales of campaigns long ended. He stands with his kinsman Amandir for the King, saying it is meet that an old man should see the old oath fulfilled ere he is laid in stone.

Anaratan, great-uncle to Lord Vorondir, is the living chronicle of Garvirionath, having ridden in his youth with Ecthelion the Second against the Corsairs at the haven of Pelargir. Sixty winters have whitened his hair but not dimmed the iron in his glance, and the household defers to his counsel in matters of lineage and oath. He holds firm with Denethor, saying that an old house keeps its word though the heavens fall.

Falathwen was born of a knightly house of Anfalas, the wind-bitten Langstrand, and was betrothed to Orondir when both were yet children, the alliance sworn between their fathers ere the eastern war took Baranor. She is gentle of bearing but resolute, and has borne her young lord twin children before her own four and twentieth year. She follows him in his fealty to the Steward.

Orweniel, daughter of Orondir and Falathwen, was born with her twin brother Talendir under the harvest-moon of a year of dark tidings. At fourteen she is already tall, grey-eyed and quiet, and has begun her lessons in the lore of her foremothers of Belfalas. The household reckons that the line of Baranionath shall not fail while she yet draws breath.

Talendir, twin-brother to Orweniel, is fourteen and the hope of Baranionath, fair-haired after his mother and grey-eyed after his sire. He rides daily upon the strand at Edhellond and is taught the sword by old men who served his grandfather. In the quarrel of these days he knows only that his father stands with the Steward, and that is enough.

Orondir, Lord of Baranionath, came to the headship of his house at nineteen, when his father Baranor was slain upon the eastern shore of Anduin in a sortie against Ithilien orc-bands. Now two and twenty, he rules the coastal fastness of his fathers at Edhellond in southern Belfalas, and the weight of an ancient name lies heavy upon young shoulders. He bears Calanaith, his father's blade, recovered with grim cost from the field where Baranor fell, and the swan-prowed ships of his haven answer to his horn. In the gathering quarrel he keeps faith with Lord Denethor, holding that vigilance, not hope, is the bulwark of these dark years.

Thingol, in his five-and-fiftieth year, is the elder kinsman of the house and warden of its archives, and was first sword-bearer to Rondamir's father in the campaigns along the Poros. He is grave of speech, sparing of laughter, and the names of all the fallen of the house lie graven in his memory. In council he speaks last and seldom, yet his word turns the chamber. He counsels his lord that the oath to the Steward must endure while the King is not yet come.
Thandirion, Warden-captain of the Naith, commands the hidden crossings of the Celebrant and answers only to the Lord and Lady of the Galadhrim.
Baranthir keeps the northern eaves of the Golden Wood, where his patrols have turned back orc-bands out of Moria beyond counting.
Aeglossen is counted among the surest bows of the Galadhrim; it is said no shaft of his has ever been found far from a foe.
Nimlothiel orders the provisioning of the wardens upon the borders, and the talans of the Naith stand ready at her word.
Malthorn leads Nos Malgalad, a house that has not forgotten Amdir who fell at Dagorlad, and keeps that memory sharp upon its spears.
Galuvir of the Egladil drills the young of the Golden Wood in blade and bow against the gathering dark in Dol Guldur.
Silivren tends the stores and songs of Nos Malgalad alike, for in Lorien the two have never been far apart.

Mauhoshat was hammered into a captain in the marshalling camps of Udun, where the legions of the Morannon are sorted and counted before the long march out. He took the Arki standard by goading three rivals into a knife-quarrel and walking out of the pit alone, a tale the muster-clerks of Lugburz are said to have written down. He covets the favour of the Great Eye above all, and trains his uruks to be noticed by the wraiths who ride down from the iron gate. The Ikhon under Maugrukh he names a company of pit-rats, for they reported his muster-count light at the last great gathering.

Maugrukh commands the watcher-tower of Cirith Ungol, that high paranoid roost above the Morgul Vale where Shelob lairs in the under-passes. He took the tower by cutting down the previous captain on the stair, an old quarrel about a shipment of mail looted from the tarks at Osgiliath. The Eye sees little of him there, and he likes it so, for a captain far from Lugburz may eat his own ghash and answer to none. He hates Mauhoshat of Udun, who once named his garrison a kennel of snaga.

Rûklash holds his banner in the slag-pits and forges of Gorgoroth, under the red light of Orodruin, where his sire was a taskmaster of the bellows. He clawed up out of the labour-gangs by breaking the captain who had flogged him as a snaga, and dragged the body up the slag-heap so the smiths would see who walked down. The men of Gondor know nothing of him yet, but the smith-orcs name him the Hammer of the Pit. He despises the Arki of Udun, who he says do nothing but stand in lines and be counted.
Shelgra rides the Dagorlad as a scout-captain for the Gate, and brings back more heads than reports.
Brûga oversees the weapon-pits behind the Black Gate, and flogs any smith-snaga who lets a blade go dull.
Nazgra is a venom-tongued archer of the wall, feared in the barracks more than on the field.
Ushka leads a raiding-pack that strikes north from the Gate, and answers the muster only when it suits her.

Thûrak stands sentinel at the Morannon, the iron Black Gate where the legions of Lugburz pour out into the northern wastes. Fear of the Great Eye is the marrow of him, for he was once flogged on the gate-stones for letting a tark scout slip past in the dusk. Since that day he has not slept the whole night through, and his uruks know better than to be found drowsing on the wall. The Brughash of Dûrzan he watches with a particular dread, for they keep their own counsel in the south and do not answer the muster as swiftly as the Gate would like.
Grublat is a gate-captain of the Morannon, a heavy-handed uruk who counts the muster with his fists. He has broken more of his own snaga than any tark ever has.
Mazgûr keeps the watch-fires on the northern wall of the Black Gate, a sharp-eyed archer who trusts no shadow that moves out on the Dagorlad.
Ufthak clawed his way up from the slave-gangs of Udun to a banner of his own, and means to drown the memory of the lash in the blood of Men.
Lugrod is an old killer of the Morannon garrison, slow to anger and slower to forgive, who has outlived three captains by being the last orc standing on the wall.
Vûshka keeps the tally of the Nurn thralls, and culls the count herself when the books run long.
Krimpa breaks the new-taken slaves of Harad and the East, and is proud that few of them survive her breaking.
Lhakra rides the pen-borders hunting runaways, and brings them back in pieces as a lesson to the rest.
Grisha oversees the poison-fields of southern Nurn, where the air itself does most of the killing.

Uznash is an overseer-captain of the Nurn slave-pens, where the thralls of Harad and the East break their backs to feed the legions. He came up through the whip-gangs, and his hatred of Men is a cold practiced thing, learned on the fields and not in any battle. The horse-boys of the Mark have never heard of him, and that is a wound he means to repair when the great muster comes. He has an old quarrel with Gûlnak of the Arki, who named his uruks farm-snaga at a Udun counting.
Durbgûl is a whip-captain of the Nurn pens, who measures a thrall's worth by how long it lasts under the lash.
Snagrat drives the field-gangs of Nurn from horseback, and has never once walked among the slaves he herds.
Hrakmaw guards the granaries that feed the legions, a brutal quartermaster who hangs hoarders from the storehouse beams.
Gorbûz came up through the whip-gangs beside Uznash, and resents that the pens answer to his old comrade and not to him.
Yagûl carries word between Barad-dur and the Morgul Vale, and has seen the inside of the Tower more than once.
Skraa keeps the under-cells of the Tower-guard, where the questioning is done and seldom finished quickly.
Murgha leads a night-pack along the Mordor road, and it is said the Eye itself favours her cruelty.
Lozka watches the Cirith Ungol garrison on Dûrzan's behalf, and counts their failings against the day she takes their pass.

Dûrzan commands a Tower-guard company in the shadow of Barad-dur itself, chosen for cunning over bulk by an officer of the Mouth's household. Payback is the engine of him, for a Morgul-captain reported his company light at a muster three years past and his banner was nearly broken for it. That captain is dead now in a stair-quarrel none can quite explain, and Dûrzan has been seen at the Mouth's gate more than once since. He keeps a particular eye on the Cirith Ungol garrison, and on Maugrukh's accounting of the dead.
Razhûk stands a Tower-guard company beneath Barad-dur, chosen for cunning, and trusts none of his own captains.
Mûzgash patrols the stairs below the Dark Tower, a silent killer who reports straight to the Mouth's household.
Bolgrat holds a watchpost on the road to Cirith Ungol, and feuds quietly with the tower garrison over the counting of the dead.
Throkka is a brute of the Tower-guard, kept for the work that wants no cunning, only weight and a heavy blade.

Gûlnak stands at Mauhoshat's right hand in the Udun camps, and the clerks of Lugburz mark him as the sharper blade of the two. He has been passed over twice for a banner of his own, and the resentment of it sits behind his teeth like a second tongue. He waits for Mauhoshat to be summoned to the Black Gate or thinned in the Pelennor, and reckons the Arki muster will fall to him before the next great war-march. Until that day he flatters his captain and counts his rivals.

Thûlnar serves as Maugrukh's lieutenant on the Cirith Ungol stair, and he has counted every coin in the captain's strongbox twice. Loot is his drive and the tower his hunting-ground, for caravans bound from Minas Morgul up to the pass are easily skimmed by the orcs who watch the road. He pays his uruks in trinkets stolen from the men of Gondor, and keeps the heavier plunder for a day when Maugrukh slips on the stair. He nurses an old grudge against Kûragh of the Akheth, who once stole his share of a Morgul-train.

Kûragh of the Akheth is Rûklash's foremost uruk in the Gorgoroth forges, and the smith-snaga fear him more than the bellows. Plunder is his sickness, and he has been known to march his company up the Morgul road on private errands of robbery. He took a fat share from a Cirith Ungol train two winters past, and Thûlnar has not forgotten it. He watches Rûklash for any sign of weakness, and reckons that a hammer-captain who tires at the anvil will not last a march to the Black Gate.

Gildor Inglorion of the House of Finrod has long wandered the westlands; in these darkening days his company keeps to Imladris and the banner of Glorfindel.
Erestor, chief of the counsellors of the house of Elrond, sets aside the ledger for the sword when the passes of the Misty Mountains grow restless.
Lindir of Imladris, quicker to song than to war, has nonetheless learned the ways of blade and bow as the Wild grows bold.

Dorwen came to the House of Olindurionath out of a lesser fief upon the windward coast of Anfalas, where the huntsmen reckon their kindred by the seasons of the seal-hunt rather than by the rolls of Minas Tirith. Three and thirty winters she has counted, and she has not unlearned the sea-wisdom of her father's strand, nor the silence that the long coast teaches. She walks with the King's faction as her wedded house does, holding that the Langstrand has waited too long upon a City that forgets its further shores.

Eleneth, second of the wedded ladies of the House of Olindurionath, was given in alliance out of an old huntsmen-line of the Anfalas coast, and she is thirty winters told. She keeps a small reliquary of weathered driftwood said to bear the mark of a Númenórean keel cast up in the year of the Dimming, and she names it her dower above any gold. She holds, with her house, for the King returned, for the wind-bitten shore has long memory and longer hope, and the watchers of the Langstrand would see the old line restored.

Hirilwen of the House of Olindurionath, eight and forty years of age, never wedded, and is named among her kindred the watch-lady of the western tower. Through the salt-rimed nights of her middle years she has trimmed the lamp that warns the fisherfolk of the long reef, and she keeps in a chest of black oak the hunting-knife of her brother who fell upon the dunes in the corsair raid of her youth. She holds, as her house holds, for the King returned, for the Langstrand has too often watched alone.

Talborin, fifty winters told, wedded into the House of Olindurionath out of a kindred-hall of the Langstrand, and he bears upon his shield the grey gull of his fathers quartered with the device of his wife's line. In his youth he sailed with the watch-galleys that ward the long coast against the corsair sail, and a scar of that work yet runs from his temple to his jaw. He stands with his house for the King returned, for he has watched too many years of vigilance go unrewarded by the lords of the inland City.

Derufin of the House of Danuhirionath, three and thirty winters of age, was reared in the shadowed dales of Morthond beneath the stern crags that look toward the Paths of the Dead. He bears the long yew bow of his fathers, and his arm is counted among the surest of Duinhir's archer-country, where the old oaths of watchfulness are not lightly set aside. With the stern lords of the Blackroot Vale he stands by Lord Denethor, holding that in the hour the shadow gathers the realm must keep one hand upon the helm, and that hand the Steward's.
Aredhel, a bold huntress of the clan, evokes the White Lady of Noldor from lore, leading swift strikes against encroaching shadows in Mirkwood's depths.
Arien, named after the sun-maia, brings fiery resolve to Nos Alenwé, her leadership piercing the darkness like dawn's first light.
Arindor, a wise navigator, guides the clan through forgotten paths, his knowledge rooted in the migrations of the Eldar.

Azgar, the Warlord of Gundabad, is a fearsome orc chieftain who rules the northern orc stronghold with an iron fist, echoing the dark legacy of Azog and Bolg from Tolkien's tales. Towering and scarred from countless battles, he unites the clans through sheer brutality and cunning, harboring a deep-seated grudge against the Dwarves who once claimed Gundabad as their own. As the primary leader, Azgar plots to reclaim the Misty Mountains' peaks, serving the growing shadow in the East while crushing any dissent among his kin.
Beleg, a strong bowman of Nos Oropher, draws from the lore of Beleg Strongbow, friend to Túrin, excelling in forest ambushes against orc incursions.
Bolgath leads his clan with the vengeful spirit of Bolg from The Hobbit, seeking to avenge ancient defeats. His aggressive expansion pushes Gundabad's borders southward.

Borzak acts as a beast-tamer in Gundabad, handling wargs and trolls akin to those allied with orcs in Tolkien's battles. His command over these creatures enhances the clan's military might in assaults.

Tharzog, a shrewd and savage leader, commands his Uruk-hai with a ruthless efficiency that embodies Isengard's dark might. His loyalty to Saruman is matched by his cunning, orchestrating battles with a keen eye for exploiting any flaw in his enemies' defenses. Bruzgash's harsh demeanor and unrelenting drive inspire dread in both allies and foes, his forces a relentless tide of destruction. Under his banner, the Black Echelon spreads fear, furthering Saruman's dominion with every brutal conquest.
Calathiel, consort to Alenon, embodies the starlight grace of Varda, her visions aiding the clan in evading Sauron's watchful gaze.

A noble Elf-lord of Lothlórien, born beneath the golden boughs of the mallorn trees. Wise beyond his years, he served as a warden of the Golden Wood and counselor to Lady Galadriel. His keen mind and steadfast heart earned him renown among the Galadhrim. Though he seldom drew his blade, his presence alone inspired calm and courage. Caurmínas was said to walk often beneath moonlit leaves, speaking softly to the trees of ancient days. When the Shadow rose once more, he stood unbroken, a guardian of light and memory, ever faithful to the spirit of Lothlórien.

Celeborn, the wise and noble Lord of Lothlórien, stands as a stalwart defender of his realm and people. Renowned for his calm demeanor and keen insight, he is a master of strategy and diplomacy, a complement to the ethereal power of Galadriel. Celeborn's presence in Lothlórien is a beacon of stability and strength, providing wise counsel to those who seek guidance. While his sword remains ever ready to protect his homeland, his true strength lies in his enduring patience and deep understanding of the struggles facing Middle-earth. Celeborn's leadership ensures that Lothlórien remains a bastion of hope amidst a world in turmoil.
Daeron, a loremaster of Nos Oropher, preserves the songs and histories of the Sindar migration, using knowledge to bolster the clan's resilience against Mirkwood's corruption.
Dagnir, a slayer of shadows, embodies the enduring spirit of the Firstborn, combating ancient evils lurking since the world's awakening.

Dáin Ironfoot, the stalwart and unyielding King under the Mountain, stands as a paragon of dwarven resilience and valor. Renowned for his unwavering determination and tactical prowess, Dáin is a battle-hardened leader who inspires loyalty and courage in his kin. A veteran of countless conflicts, he led the dwarves of the Iron Hills with unmatched strength, bringing stability and prosperity to his people. His resolve in the face of adversity and his dedication to the defense of Erebor and its allies ensure that the legacy of Durin's folk endures through the darkest days of the Third Age.
Drazgor, a wraith-like commander, haunts the borders of Mirkwood, his ethereal form striking terror like the Nazgûl in the films, enforcing Sauron's will through fear and illusion.

Drozmak is a savage orc captain in Gundabad, known for his relentless raids on Dwarven outposts, much like the orc hordes that assailed Erebor in the books. His tactical ferocity and loyalty to Azgar make him a key enforcer, ensuring clan unity through intimidation and bloodshed, ever eager to spill the blood of Elves and Men encroaching on orc territories.

Drûgash, a cunning and iron-willed leader of the Black Maw, commands his Uruk-hai with a blend of calculated strategy and raw aggression. His devotion to Saruman fuels his relentless drive, his forces sweeping across Middle-earth with disciplined savagery. Drûgash's sharp intellect and scorn for weakness make him a formidable commander, his troops a relentless engine of destruction. Under his leadership, the Black Maw carves a path of ruin, advancing Isengard's dark ambitions with every bloody triumph.
Druzhak, a spirit caller, summons ghosts, evoking the haunted aura of the fortress in lore.

Druznar is a veteran orc fighter, scarred from clashes reminiscent of the Battle of Azanulbizar. In Gundabad, he trains new recruits, instilling the hatred and skills needed to confront the Dwarves once more.
Druznia, a spectral consort, haunts dreams, her influence spreading fear like the Nazgûl's Black Breath.
Dulruk, a terror rider, patrols from above, spotting and striking with precision.
Durga, a resilient orc warrior-female, embodies the tough endurance of orc kind in harsh environments. She guards the inner sanctums, ensuring the clan's core remains unbreached.
Durkar, a spectral lieutenant, aids in raising wraiths, her presence chilling like the fear induced by the Necromancer in Mirkwood's lore.
Durla, a shadow binder, manipulates darkness, concealing guards as in Dol Guldur's veiled assaults.

Durmash is a stalwart orc guardian of Gundabad's halls, evoking the vigilant orcs that guarded the passes in Middle-earth's lore. His defensive prowess protects the stronghold from intruders, while his alliance with clan members strengthens the internal bonds against external threats.
Durmorg, a brood keeper, raises spiderlings, bolstering Khamûl's creepy allies.
Durzak is a vanguard orc, leading charges with the fury of Uglúk's band. In Gundabad, his boldness breaks enemy lines in pivotal battles.
Durzha, a resurrectionist, revives the slain, bolstering Khamûl's endless armies.
Elbereth, invoking Varda's name, leads with celestial hymns, her clan drawing strength from ancient Avari roots in the deep woods.

Chägermeister, last scion of the Nolimar—guardians of Elvenkind's forgotten wisdom—is both warrior and sage. Born of Maegorn the peerless blade and Lúthiel the luminous scholar, his parents vanished with Gondolin's fall. He carries the final ember of their legacy. Under Elrond's counsel, he wanders not merely to uncover his kin's fate, but to reignite the flame of a fading Elvendom. He is the living bridge between lost ages and the hope of a reborn Elven legacy. This hero honors a high-rank Patreon supporter of TAOM whose patronage has sustained the mod for numerous months.

Elrond, the Lord of Rivendell, is a figure of unmatched wisdom, healing, and foresight. As a descendant of both Elves and Men, he bridges the two worlds with grace and understanding. Rivendell, under his guidance, stands as a sanctuary of knowledge and refuge for all who seek aid in their struggle against the shadow. Elrond's insight shapes the great councils of the Free Peoples, and his stewardship over the Last Homely House ensures that the light of the Eldar continues to shine. In both counsel and action, he exemplifies the timeless strength and resilience of the Elves.

Ethacali Cilzeron, a diplomatic envoy of Rhûn, negotiates treaties and alliances in the Third Age to expand Sauron's influence. His eloquence and cunning secure vital pacts. Ethacali's words weave a net of loyalty around the Easterling clans.

Feren, a loyal captain in Thranduil's guard, reflects the steadfast warriors seen in the films, patrolling the borders with unmatched archery skill. His devotion to the Elvenking ensures the safety of the halls, warding off spiders and orcs with precision and valor.
Finduilas, consort to Taurion, channels the tragic beauty of her namesake from the Silmarillion, her healing arts sustaining river guardians against Dol Guldur's poisons.

Galadriel, the Lady of Lothlórien, is a being of extraordinary grace, wisdom, and power. As one of the eldest and most revered Elves in Middle-earth, she wields unmatched foresight and a profound connection to the unseen world. Galadriel's strength lies not in martial might but in her unwavering resolve to preserve beauty and hope against the encroaching shadow. Her leadership transforms Lothlórien into a haven of serenity and light, and her guidance inspires unity and courage among the Free Peoples of Middle-earth. Through her wisdom and the radiance of Nenya, she embodies the enduring spirit of resistance against darkness.
Galenor, chieftain of Nos Galengrim, focuses on Mirkwood's green heart, combating the forest's decay with wards akin to those against Sauron's influence in the books.

Galion, the royal butler and advisor, evokes the merry yet dutiful elves in The Hobbit, managing the feasts and stores of the Woodland Realm. His resourcefulness supports the clan's endurance, blending mirth with the serious defense against encroaching evils.

Gorlag, a towering and merciless warlord of the Black Maw, rules his Uruk-hai with an unyielding grip, his loyalty to Saruman matched only by his thirst for slaughter. His commanding presence and brutal tactics ensure that his forces strike with overwhelming force, leaving no survivors in their wake. Gorlag's disdain for mercy and his strategic prowess make him a terror to Middle-earth's defenders, his victories a testament to Isengard's might. With the Black Maw at his back, he drives Saruman's war machine forward, crushing all opposition.
Gorvash, a beast mistress, tames draconic horrors, her command echoing the dread steeds' shrieks.
Gorzag, an orc warlord, rallies hordes for Khamûl, his ferocity mirroring the orc captains in The Hobbit, pushing incursions into elven territories.

Gragor acts as a ruthless orc overseer in Gundabad, enforcing discipline akin to the taskmasters in Mordor's armies from the books. His role in managing the clan's forges and slaves ensures a steady supply of weapons, bolstering the horde's readiness for the impending wars.
Gralnia, a necromantic healer, sustains the wounded, twisting life to unlife for Khamûl's service.
Gralthak, an orc duelist, thrives in single combats like the orc champions in lore. His prowess in challenges asserts clan dominance in internal disputes and external battles.

Gralza, a fierce orc matron of Gundabad, draws from the implied shadowy breeders in Tolkien's world, overseeing the rearing of new warriors with iron resolve. Her strategic mind aids in clan politics, ensuring the survival and proliferation of orc kind amidst the northern perils.
Gralzia, a shadow infiltrator, spies in darkness, like the unseen agents of Sauron.
Gralzuk, a silk harvester, crafts traps from webs, aiding in capturing elven scouts as in film scenes.
Grasha, a death whisperer, demoralizes enemies, her voice like the chilling winds from Dol Guldur in the films.
Grazar serves as a beast-master, taming giant spiders akin to those in Mirkwood. In Gundabad, his pets guard tunnels and ensnare intruders.

Sharku, a fierce and calculating leader, commands his Uruk-hai with a blend of brute force and sharp intellect. His allegiance to Saruman drives him to crush any who oppose Isengard's might, his troops forged into a relentless war machine under his exacting standards. Gurzod's cold pragmatism and utter lack of pity make him a dreaded foe, his strategies leaving enemies broken and scattered. With every triumph, he strengthens Isengard's grip, embodying the Red Echelon's merciless resolve.
Haldir, a border sentinel, mirrors the Lórien marchwardens in the books, patrolling with silent precision to thwart spider nests along the riverbanks.
Iminyar, elder of Nos Iminyé, traces lineage to the first-awakened elves, preserving primal Silvan traditions against Mirkwood's taint.

Kargoth, a brutal orc warrior of Gundabad, embodies the merciless spirit of Tolkien's orcs, forged in the pits of Angband's descendants. He leads scouting parties into the wilds, ambushing travelers and gathering intelligence for Azgar's campaigns, his hatred for the Free Peoples burning as fiercely as the forges beneath the mountains.
Kargul, a claw master, trains beasts for combat, rending armor like the fell beasts' talons.
Kazla, a arcane enforcer, punishes disloyalty, maintaining order in Khamûl's shadowed halls.
Kaznia, a rune scribe, inscribes wards, fortifying the tower with dark enchantments.
Kazrag, a curse-bringer, afflicts foes with plagues, mirroring the sickness that befell Greenwood in the books.
Kazria, a fear monger, instills dread, mirroring the morale-crushing presence of the Nazgûl.
Korgul is a lieutenant of the Black Echelon who rose by outlasting the uruks placed above him. He gives an order once and looks for the axe if it is not obeyed.
Kragloth commands a Gundabad sub-clan with the ferocity of Bolg's lieutenants in The Hobbit. His focus on mountain warfare makes him a master of ambushes in the high passes, targeting trade routes.
Kralza, a commanding orc female, oversees training grounds with the authority of a captain. Her drills produce relentless fighters for the horde.
Krogar is a marauder orc, leading pillaging bands reminiscent of those that ravaged the Shire's borders. His hauls sustain the clan's war machine.
Krozar, a lurker chief, ambushes from trees, like the spiders that ensnared Bilbo's company.
Kruznor is a strategist orc, planning incursions with the cunning of Grishnákh from the books. His schemes exploit weaknesses in Dwarven defenses.
Kzha, a lich-like mage, extends unlife, reflecting Sauron's immortality pursuits.

Legolas, son of Thranduil, is a masterful archer and scout, as depicted in both books and films, venturing beyond Mirkwood to aid the Free Peoples with his keen senses and unerring aim against the forces of darkness.

Leôrdinoth Kalkian, a veteran campaigner of Rhûn, leads seasoned warriors into battle during the Third Age for Sauron. His experience turns the tide in many conflicts. Leôrdinoth's tactical genius maximizes the Easterlings' martial prowess.
Morgrub, the Great Goblin of Blue Craig, whose swarms infest the Blue Mountains of the far west, hard by the Grey Havens of Lindon.
Muzgash, the Great Goblin of Goblin Town, master of the warrens of the High Pass.
Krazdra leads scouting parties for the Iron Fist. Her knowledge of the terrain surrounding Isengard is unmatched.
Ughasha commands the Blood Guard's forward sentries. Her vigilance has foiled many attempts to infiltrate Isengard's defenses.
Bolga is the Skull Crushers' champion, having bested every challenger in the fighting pits. Her strength is legendary among the Uruk-hai.
Snarla keeps the forges of the Ash Guard burning day and night. Her weapons arm the armies that march from Isengard.
Grisnak earned his command through brutality and cunning during countless raids. His knowledge of Rohan's borderlands makes him invaluable for lightning strikes against enemy supply lines.
Muzgash leads the feared berserker units of Isengard. His warriors paint themselves with the blood of enemies before battle, striking terror into those who face them.
Morgash rose through the ranks as master of reconnaissance. His scouts range far ahead of Isengard's armies, marking targets for destruction.
Krûklash maintains discipline among the Uruk-hai with an iron fist. Those who disobey his orders rarely live to regret their mistake.
Dûshrat proved his worth in single combat against dozens of challengers. He now leads the elite guard of the White Hand.
Gashnak is a fierce Uruk-hai warrior who earned her place through brutal combat. She commands the breeding pits of Isengard with ruthless efficiency.
Radzga orchestrates raids for the Shadow Reavers. She strikes without warning and vanishes before the enemy can regroup.
Lugara trains the warg packs of the War Hounds. Her beasts follow her commands with unwavering obedience.
Shank can track prey across any terrain. His hunters never return empty-handed, whether pursuing game or fleeing enemies.
Urbash's bloodlust is legendary even among the Uruk-hai. He collects the heads of worthy opponents as trophies of his victories.
Ufthak leads devastating mounted raids deep into enemy territory. His warg riders strike without warning and vanish before retaliation arrives.
Gragnor trains the warg packs of Isengard. His beasts are said to understand commands as well as any soldier.
Narzug commands the largest warg pack in Isengard's armies. His riders form the vanguard of every major assault.
Muzgura rose through the ranks of the Red Echelon by her cunning and ferocity. She oversees the war preparations of her company.
Sharlug is a battle-hardened lieutenant of the Black Echelon. Her tactical instincts have saved her company from ambush many times.
Grisha engineers the siege weapons of the Stone Breakers. Her constructions have brought down many a fortress wall.
Thraka serves the Black Maw as quartermaster and enforcer. Her iron discipline keeps the supply lines running even under siege.
Círdan, the Shipwright, Lord of the Grey Havens and eldest of the Eldar in Middle-earth, who kept the Ring Narya until he gave it to Mithrandir.
Bûrzum, Warlord of the Misty Mountains, who holds the deep places of Moria and the cold peaks above.
Zimraphel, a descendant of the Black Númenóreans, commands the Corsair fleet with cunning and grace. Her knowledge of the sea and its treacherous currents is unrivaled among the captains of Umbar.
Lorgath, master of the Black Spider Horde, breeds giant spiders, directly inspired by the arachnids of Mirkwood in The Hobbit.

Lothuial, consort to Thranduil, draws from the elegant elven queens in Middle-earth's tales, providing counsel and healing wisdom to the royal house. Her presence strengthens the bonds of Nos Lasgalen, fostering unity among the Wood-elves as they confront the darkness spreading through Mirkwood.
Lugburz is scoutmaster of the White Hand, and the maps of the Gap of Rohan are kept in his head rather than on paper. He sends his runners out in threes and expects two back.

Lugdush, grim commander of the Black Echelon, is a brutal enforcer of Saruman's doctrine. Towering and iron-clad, he drills his soldiers into a wall of shields and steel, smashing opposition with unflinching discipline. Unlike his berserker kin, Lugdush values structure over rage—his warriors are trained, not frenzied. He speaks little but strikes decisively, and his presence on the battlefield signals a cold, inevitable advance. Among the Uruk-hai, Lugdush is feared not for his voice, but for the silence that follows his command.
Lurthak is a brawler orc, engaging in pit fights that mirror the brutal orc recreations in the tales. His strength bolsters the clan's frontline in massive melees.

Lurtz, the savage chieftain of the Black Maw, is the embodiment of raw Uruk ferocity. Bred for strength and domination, he leads his berserker warband with a thirst for slaughter unmatched even among the White Hand. Lurtz scorns restraint—his warriors fight in brutal packs, tearing through enemy ranks with overwhelming violence. Though he lacks the finesse of Saruman's other captains, few can rival his battlefield presence. Driven by fury and instinct, Lurtz and the Black Maw are loosed only when Saruman demands utter annihilation.
Lurzia, a spell sentinel, detects magic, countering elven sorcery in Mirkwood's conflicts.

Lurzok, an orc archer captain, draws from the bow-wielding orcs that harried travelers in Middle-earth lore. His volleys from the mountain heights defend Gundabad's approaches, picking off scouts from Dwarven or Elven parties.

Mauhúr, captain of the Red Echelon, is a relentless tactician forged in the blood pits beneath Isengard. Clad in iron, he commands the vanguard of Saruman's war host with ruthless precision. Mauhúr believes victory is won not by strength alone, but by the cold execution of orders. His warband is always first into the breach, driving fear into the hearts of men with disciplined aggression and merciless efficiency. To Mauhúr, hesitation is failure—and failure is death. Under his command, the Red Echelon carves a path of destruction worthy of the White Hand.
Mazkor is a tracker orc, hunting prey with the keen senses of Tolkien's orc hunters. In Gundabad, he pursues escaped slaves and spies, maintaining the clan's security.
Morgra, a venom spitter, enhances beasts with poisons, deadly as Sauron's corrupted creatures.
Morgulash, a shadowy sorceress, weaves dark spells in Dol Guldur, her arts reminiscent of the necromancy that corrupted the hill fortress in the books, aiding Khamûl in summoning undead minions.
Morzag, a bone collector, crafts totems of power, drawing from the foul rituals in Dol Guldur's shadows.

Mugzun is a heavy-handed orc enforcer, reminiscent of the whip-wielding orcs in the books' slave pits. In Gundabad, he maintains order among the ranks, crushing rebellions and ensuring unwavering obedience to the clan's directives.
Muzra is an orc herbalist, brewing potions from foul ingredients in Middle-earth's corrupted lands. Her elixirs enhance warriors' endurance in prolonged fights.
Muzrak, a curse caster, afflicts intruders, his hexes weakening foes like Sauron's debilitating influence.
Narduk, a sky scourge, leads aerial assaults, diving upon foes like the Nazgûl attacks in lore.

Nargoth, a raiding orc warlord, embodies the pillaging hordes that sacked settlements in the North. His expeditions bring back slaves and spoils, enriching the clan and fueling the endless cycle of orcish aggression.
Nargra is an orc poisoner, crafting toxins inspired by the foul arts in Middle-earth lore. Her venoms weaken enemies before battles, tilting the odds in Gundabad's favor.
Nargrash, a web weaver, ensnares prey for Khamûl, her tactics mimicking the spider ambushes in the books.
Narlog, a lore-keeper orc, recites tales of ancient grudges against Dwarves, inspired by Tolkien's deep orc history. He rallies the clan with stories of past glories and future vengeance.
Narsha, a dark enchantress, curses enemies with sorcery, her magic reflecting the corrupting influence of Dol Guldur on the forest in the tales.
Narzia, a wraith binder, enslaves souls, bolstering Khamûl's ethereal forces.
Narzog is a harasser orc, using hit-and-run tactics from the lore of orc skirmishers. His mobility keeps pressure on neighboring realms.
Narzugh, overlord of the Necromancer's Legion, summons undead legions, embodying Sauron's necromantic experiments in Dol Guldur from the appendices.
Narzuk serves as a messenger orc, carrying decrees swiftly like the runners in Sauron's armies. His speed ensures coordinated strikes across the mountains.

Neida Zorian, a spiritual guide of Rhûn, inspires fanatical devotion to Sauron among her clan in the Third Age. Her rituals strengthen the warriors' resolve. Neida's faith unites the Easterlings in unholy purpose.
Nellas, a woodland guide, draws from the elf who aided Túrin, her tracking skills uncovering hidden paths and threats in the tangled woods.
Nimrien, a swift messenger, carries tidings across Mirkwood, her agility evoking the fleet-footed elves of old lore.
Nimrodel, named after the legendary elf-maid from lore, serves as a healer and scout in Nos Lasgalen, her knowledge of herbs and paths aiding in the protection of Mirkwood's ancient secrets.

Oropherion, leader of Nos Oropher, honors the legacy of Thranduil's father Oropher, slain in the Last Alliance, by commanding veteran Sindar warriors in defense of Mirkwood's northern borders against Angmar's remnants.
Orophin, a vigilant archer, stands watch like the border guards in films, his arrows felling beasts corrupted by Mirkwood's shadows.

Rukthar, a grim and indomitable warlord of the Black Echelon, leads his Uruk-hai with a chilling blend of discipline and cruelty. His unwavering devotion to Saruman fuels his relentless campaigns, his forces striking with precision and terror under his command. Rukthar's disdain for weakness and his strategic brilliance make him a fearsome adversary, his troops a scourge upon Middle-earth's Free Peoples. With a heart as cold as Isengard's forges, he advances Saruman's ambitions, leaving only ruin in his wake.
Rumil, a scholar and warrior, preserves ancient grimoires, using knowledge to forge defenses against the Necromancer's curses.

Rurazaur Bozorganith, a beast-master of Rhûn, commands fearsome creatures in battle during the Third Age for Sauron. His bond with wild beasts sows chaos among foes. Rurazaur's monstrous allies amplify the terror of the Easterling assaults.
Taurion, warden of Nos Taurion, oversees the Forest River's defenses, inspired by the enchanted waters in The Hobbit, protecting trade and borders from southern threats.
Thalion, a mighty warrior, channels the strength of ancient heroes, defending the clan's star-gazing clearings from nocturnal assaults.
Thalka, a web strategist, plans entanglements, trapping foes in Dol Guldur's schemes.
Thalrug serves as a cavalry orc rider, commanding warg packs akin to those in the Battle of Five Armies. His swift strikes harass foes from afar, extending Gundabad's reach.
Thorzag, a fang master, commands spider assaults, echoing the battles in Mirkwood.
Thrakgul oversees the Black Maw's pit-gangs and counts a shift wasted if nothing is broken in it. Saruman's overseers leave him to his methods because the mail comes out on time.

Thranduil, the Elvenking of the Woodland Realm, is a wise and stern ruler, embodying the grace and resilience of the Sindar elves from Tolkien's lore. As the son of Oropher, he guards Mirkwood against the encroaching shadows of Dol Guldur, leading with a keen strategic mind and unyielding defense of his forested domain, ever vigilant in the face of Sauron's growing threat.

Thrangul, a twisted orc chieftain in the Shadow Tower Clan, serves Khamûl with brutal efficiency, leading raids that echo the orc assaults in Tolkien's tales, sowing fear among the Wood-elves of Mirkwood.
Thrargol, a grave robber, desecrates tombs for Khamûl, fueling the undead hordes as hinted in Sauron's dark arts.

Thrazak serves as a hardened orc lieutenant in Gundabad, drawing from the lore of orcish hordes that plagued the North. His skill in siege warfare and unyielding aggression make him indispensable in assaults on fortified positions, always striving to expand Gundabad's domain under the Warlord's command.
Thrazgul, a tormentor orc, extracts information from captives, akin to the interrogators in Tolkien's dark realms. His methods yield valuable intelligence for the clan.
Throrgash, chieftain of the Fell Beast Tribe, breeds winged terrors, inspired by the fell beasts ridden by Nazgûl in books and films.
Thrugash, a screech caller, unnerves enemies, her beasts' cries breaking morale as in battles.
Thrugol, an orc smith, hammers armor echoing the dark forges of Isengard. In Gundabad, his works clad warriors in impenetrable plates for the coming wars.
Thrulza, a vigilant orc sentinel, watches the passes like the guards of Cirith Ungol. Her alertness thwarts infiltrations into Gundabad's depths.
Thrulzia, a ghost whisperer, communes with spirits, summoning aid from beyond the grave.

Thrumak is a forge-master orc, forging weapons in the style of those used by Azog's forces in the movies and books. His craftsmanship arms Gundabad's warriors, turning raw ore into instruments of war and destruction.
Thrunak, an orc infiltrator, sneaks into enemy camps like the spies in Tolkien's wars. His sabotage undermines foes from within.
Thrurg, head of the Dark Sorcerer's Guard, wields forbidden magics, guarding Khamûl with spells akin to Sauron's sorcery in lore.

Thurka is a cunning orc scout and assassin in Gundabad, embodying the stealthy prowlers that haunted the woods in the tales. Her role in espionage and sabotage weakens foes before the main assaults, contributing to Azgar's overarching strategy of domination.

Born into the noble line of the House of Caladionath, Eldorion can trace his mighty ancestry back to the ancient island kingdom of Númenor and has ever been a most noble and honorable vassal of Lord Denethor. Now, as the shadow in the east grows longer and his days grow old, he once again must take up arms, defend his liege and be the northernmost bulwark against the incoming tidal wave of darkness. And yet, through these dark days, hope remains and the banners of Lord Eldorion may fly high once more.

Tulrok Mithruntai, an innovative tactician of Rhûn, develops new warfare methods in the Third Age to serve Sauron. His inventions surprise and overwhelm enemies. Tulrok's ingenuity gives the Easterlings an edge in their campaigns.

Uglúk, the ruthless and cunning warlord of Isengard, commands Saruman's fearsome Uruk-hai with brutal efficiency. Fiercely loyal to his master, Uglúk embodies the relentless discipline and savagery that define the White Wizard's armies. Known for his harsh demeanor and unyielding resolve, he leads his troops with a mix of intimidation and tactical prowess, ensuring their dominance on the battlefield. Uglúk's disdain for weakness and his willingness to crush any opposition make him a fearsome figure among both his allies and enemies. Under his command, Isengard's forces strike terror into the hearts of the Free Peoples of Middle-earth, advancing Saruman's dark ambitions with every victory.

Ulgrim is a cunning orc tactician within Gundabad's ranks, reminiscent of the sly and treacherous orcs in The Hobbit. He orchestrates ambushes and traps, using the misty terrain to his advantage, and his loyalty to the clan fuels his desire to eradicate the lingering influence of Durin's Folk.
Ulthrak, a spider tamer, unleashes arachnid swarms, drawing from the giant spiders of Mirkwood in the books, trapping and poisoning foes in webs of darkness.
Ulzar, a nest guardian, protects lairs, ensuring the tribe's monstrous proliferation.
Ulzara is an orc seer, interpreting signs from the dark lords as in Tolkien's prophetic elements. Her visions direct the clan's fateful actions.
Ulzra, a flight commander, coordinates dives, overwhelming ground forces from the skies.
Urzara, sovereign of the Wraith Shadow Clan, manipulates shadows, akin to the Ringwraiths' terror in lore.
Urzok, a venom lord, poisons wells and arrows, spreading corruption like the spiders' taint in lore.
Urzul is a siege engineer orc, building engines of war reminiscent of Sauron's forces. In Gundabad, his contraptions batter down gates, preparing for assaults on fortified holds.

Vorgoth leads a sub-clan in Gundabad, a brutal orc chieftain inspired by the infighting orc captains in Tolkien's narratives. His ambition drives raids into Angmar's remnants, seeking artifacts of power to elevate his status within the greater horde.
Vorgria, a phantom stalker, pursues enemies unseen, evoking the relentless hunt of the Nine.
Vorgrim acts as a supply master orc, hoarding resources much like the stockpiles in orc strongholds from the books. His management sustains prolonged campaigns against the North.
Vorla, a divination seer, foresees threats, guiding the guard against Wood-elf ambushes.
Vorthak, a cursed guardian, defends the tower with undead vigor, his role akin to the barrow-wights influenced by Sauron's power in Middle-earth lore.
Vorzak commands his clan with the ambition of rising orc lords, aspiring to greater power under Sauron's shadow. His alliances forge stronger ties within Gundabad.
Vorzha is an orc healer of sorts, using crude remedies drawn from the dark knowledge in Tolkien's world. Her role sustains the wounded, allowing Gundabad's forces to recover and strike again.
Vorzul, a nest guardian, protects spider lairs, ensuring the horde's multiplication in Dol Guldur's depths.

Gurzod, a towering figure of the White Hand, leads his Uruk-hai with unyielding authority and a thirst for conquest. His devotion to Saruman fuels his relentless pursuit of victory, commanding his forces with a disciplined ferocity that leaves no room for failure. Vrothgar's strategic acumen and commanding presence make him a cornerstone of Isengard's war machine, his troops marching with grim resolve under his banner. Known for his scorn of weakness, he forges his warriors into an unstoppable force, striking dread into the hearts of Middle-earth's defenders.
Vurlak acts as a quartermaster orc, distributing gear like the logisticians in large orc armies. His efficiency keeps the clan battle-ready.
Vurzag is an orc saboteur, planting traps like those that ensnared Thorin's company. In Gundabad, his guerrilla tactics disrupt enemy movements, sowing chaos among the Free Peoples.

Yurzal Vazevian, a charismatic orator of Rhûn, rallies the masses to Sauron's banner in the Third Age. His speeches ignite passion for conquest. Yurzal's rhetoric transforms reluctant tribes into fervent warriors.

Ar-Gimilkhâd, the enigmatic and ruthless leader of Umbar, commands the Corsairs with unmatched cunning and ambition. A master strategist and a shrewd manipulator, Ar-Gimilkhâd wields both the sword and the mind with deadly precision. Under his rule, Umbar thrives as a haven for raiders and seafarers, its dark ships spreading fear across the coasts of Middle-earth. Ar-Gimilkhâd's vision of dominance extends beyond the seas, as he forges alliances with the forces of shadow and prepares to unleash the might of Umbar against the Free Peoples. His charisma and iron-fisted rule ensure loyalty among his captains, while his name strikes terror into the hearts of his enemies.

Zargoth, the ferocious warlord, leads his Uruk-hai with a savage intensity that terrifies all who face him. His absolute loyalty to Saruman drives his relentless pursuit of victory, his troops a devastating force honed by his brutal leadership. Zargoth's lack of mercy and keen tactical mind make him a scourge on the battlefield, his victories piling corpses at Isengard's gates. With every enemy crushed, he strengthens the Black Maw's fearsome reputation, serving Saruman's dark vision without hesitation.
Zargra, a poison mistress, brews venoms, enhancing the clan's deadly arsenal.
Zarkash, a fell beast handler, commands winged horrors from Dol Guldur, evoking the dread steeds of the Ringwraiths in lore, scouting and assaulting from the skies.
Zarlug, an arcane warden, erects barriers of shadow, protecting Dol Guldur as the Necromancer's illusions in the books.

Zorgath, a ferocious orc berserker, channels the raw fury of Tolkien's orc legions that clashed at the Battle of Five Armies. In Gundabad, he charges into the fray with reckless abandon, inspiring fear in enemies and respect among allies, all in service to Azgar's vision of orc supremacy.

Zorgha serves as a shamanic orc advisor, echoing the dark rituals hinted at in Tolkien's orc culture. His omens and curses bolster the clan's morale, invoking the spirits of ancient evils to aid in their conquests.
Zorgrul, an animating sorcerer, revives fallen warriors, his craft akin to Sauron's dominion over death.

Zorlag, a cunning and relentless warlord of the White Hand, drives Isengard's Uruk-hai with a fierce blend of strategy and savagery. His loyalty to Saruman is absolute, and his sharp mind ensures that every maneuver serves the White Wizard's grand designs. Zorlag's calculating nature makes him a master of exploiting enemy weaknesses, while his harsh leadership inspires both fear and obedience in his ranks. With a cold disdain for mercy, he crushes opposition with brutal precision, cementing his reputation as a formidable commander whose victories bolster Isengard's growing dominion.

Zulgara, a shrewd orc overseer, reflects the harsh survival instincts of orc females in lore. She manages the clan's breeding pits, ensuring a constant supply of warriors for the impending shadow wars.
Zulgor, a wing breeder, hatches fell eggs, expanding Khamûl's airborne dominion.
Zulgora, a shade weaver, crafts illusions, deceiving foes as Sauron's deceptions in the tales.
Zulgoth acts as a ritualist orc, performing sacrifices to dark powers as hinted in orc customs. His rites invoke strength for the clan's endeavors.
Nazgûl, the Shadow of the Northmen
